items.title: Around 10 million hectares of forest are lost each year
items.claim: How much forest does the world lose annually?

options.text: Net loss is around 4.7 million hectares per year (FAO 2020), with gross tropical deforestation of around 10 million ha/year partly offset by plantation expansion and natural regeneration in temperate regions
Around 100 million hectares lost per year

items.reveal_title: Gross loss, net loss, and what counts
items.reveal:
FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020: net forest loss of 4.7 million ha/year for 2010-2020, down from 7.8 million ha/year for 1990-2000. Tropical primary forest loss in 2022: around 4.1 million ha (Global Forest Watch).

Main drivers: cattle ranching (Amazon), palm oil (Indonesia, Malaysia), soybean expansion (Cerrado), small-holder agriculture (Congo Basin).

The distinction between primary forest and plantation matters: a monoculture plantation is not biodiverse forest, but counts as 'forest area' under FAO definitions.
items.why: Definitions shape the apparent crisis. 'Forest cover stable' can mean primary forest replaced by plantation. Following the right metric (intact primary forest, biodiversity) is essential to understand the real loss.

items.title: The Himalayas rise faster than they erode — but only just
items.claim: The Himalayas are uplifting at around 5-10 mm per year. What does this rate compare to?

options.text: Erosion is negligible; the mountains simply keep growing
Erosion roughly matches uplift in many parts of the range — the visible rate of height gain is only the difference
Erosion outpaces uplift, so the Himalayas are slowly shrinking
The mountains have been at their current height for 10 million years

items.reveal:
The India-Eurasia collision (started around 50 Ma) drives uplift. Monsoonal rainfall, glacier carving and river incision — especially by the Indus and the Brahmaputra — remove rock at comparable rates.

This is the 'aneurysm' or 'tectonic aneurysm' model: in places like Nanga Parbat, intense focused erosion actually accelerates uplift by removing load. Mountains are dynamic balance points, not static features.
items.why: Landscapes look permanent. They are conveyor belts running at millimetres per year, where the visible shape is the residual of two enormous, competing processes.
